6	\begin{hypothesis}[Homogeneous covariance]\label{H:homog}
7	  Let $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha_0 < 1$. The spatial covariance is a
8	  nonnegative, even, positive-definite tempered Radon measure $\Gamma$ on
9	  $\R^d$, with positive even tempered Radon spectral measure $\mu$ in the
10	  convention
11	  \[
12	    \Gamma=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\mu(\ud\xi)
13	    \quad\text{in the sense of tempered distributions}.
14	  \]
15	  The symbol $\gamma$ in~\eqref{E:cov} denotes this covariance as a function
16	  when one exists, and as a distribution otherwise. For every Borel set $A$ and
17	  $c > 0$, $\Gamma(cA) = c^{d-\alpha}\Gamma(A)$, and
18	  \begin{equation}\label{E:threshold}
19	    \alpha_0+\alpha<2,
20	  \end{equation}
21	  with $0 < \alpha < d$, or $\alpha = d = 1$. In particular, the last case
22	  includes spatial white noise $\Gamma = \delta_0$.
23	\end{hypothesis}
24	
25	\paragraph{Zero covariance.}
26	Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} allows $\Gamma = 0$ by design. In this case the
27	centered Gaussian noise is $\W = 0$, and the solution with initial data
28	$(1,0)$ is $u(t,x) = 1$. Thus $\E|u(t,x)|^p = 1$ for every $p > 0$, and
29	all normalized logarithmic moment rates are zero. Results asserting strict
30	positivity of covariance-dependent quantities impose $\Gamma \ne 0$ locally.

54	\section{Covariance bounds for physically masked wave fields}
55	\label{S:masked-covariance}
56	
57	We establish the covariance estimates needed for the operator construction.
58	Throughout this section, Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} holds, $a = \alpha_0$, and
59	$\Gamma \ne 0$. For zero spatial covariance, the spatial spectral measures and
60	noise variances vanish; the purely temporal estimates remain valid independently
61	of $\Gamma$. We use the unitary Fourier transform
62	\[
63	  \widehat{f}(\xi) = c_d\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\ud x,
64	  \qquad c_d = (2\pi)^{-d/2}.
65	\]
66	The spectral convention in Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} means that, for every
67	complex Schwartz test $\varphi$,
68	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-spectral-convention}
69	  \int_{\R^d}\varphi(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
70	  = \int_{\R^d}\left(\int_{\R^d}e^{i\xi\cdot x}
71	  \varphi(x)\ud x\right)\mu(\ud\xi).
72	\end{equation}
73	This is an identity of distribution pairings. We will not interchange two
74	infinite measures in the associated oscillatory expression.

81	```latex
82	\section{The unmasked Rayleigh rate and nonnegative controls}
83	\label{S:unmasked-variational}
84	
85	Fix a nonzero covariance satisfying Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, including its
86	original amplitude, and set $a = \alpha_0$. Define the full class
87	\begin{equation}\label{E:variational-positive-class}
88	  \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}
89	  =\{\Psi\in C_c^\infty((0,1)\times\R^d;\R):
90	  \Psi\ge0,\ \Psi\ne0\}.
91	\end{equation}
92	
93	\input{notes/figures/nonseparable-controls}
94	It includes nonseparable tests. It is nonempty: if $b(z) = e^{-1/(1-z^2)}$ on
95	$|z| < 1$ and zero otherwise, then $b(4s-2)\prod_{j=1}^db(x_j)$ belongs to this
96	class. All boundary derivatives vanish because exponential decay dominates every
97	power of $(1-z^2)^{-1}$. For each $\Psi$ retain the original mean $h_{\Psi,s}$
98	and original variance $v_\Psi = \E W(\Psi)^2$ from~\eqref{E:compact-raw-mean}--%
99	\eqref{E:compact-raw-cost}. Neither the test nor its covariance is changed by a
100	physical mask. We write $h_s$ when $\Psi$ is fixed.
101	
102	\subsection{Global bounds and the unmasked spectral bottom}
103	
104	\begin{lemma}[Gaussian envelope for the original covariance]
105	  \label{L:variational-heat-envelope}
106	  For the normalized heat kernel $p_\epsilon(x) =
107	  (2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/(2\epsilon)}$,
108	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-heat-envelope}
109	    (\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(x)
110	    =\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2/2}\mu(\ud\xi),
111	    \qquad
112	    0\le(\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(x)
113	    \le(\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(0)<\infty.
114	  \end{equation}
115	  The value at zero is strictly positive.
116	\end{lemma}
117	
118	\begin{proof}
119	  A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial ball growth. Indeed, evaluate
120	  its tempered bound on a nonnegative smooth cutoff equal to one on $B_1$,
121	  dilated by $R \ge 1$. Its finitely many Schwartz seminorms are bounded by
122	  $CR^N$, so positivity gives a ball-mass bound $CR^N$. Summing dyadic annuli
123	  shows that $(1+|x|)^{-L}$ is integrable for $L > N$. Apply this separately to
124	  $\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Gaussian weights are therefore integrable against both
125	  measures. The classical convolution on the left is finite and smooth locally
126	  in $x$: on compact $x$ sets its translated Gaussian derivatives are bounded by
127	  any fixed sufficiently fast polynomial weight in the integration variable.
128	
129	  Pair the convolution with a Schwartz test $\varphi$. Absolute Fubini is
130	  justified by these weights. The resulting pairing is that of $\Gamma$ with
131	  $p_\epsilon*\varphi$. Applying the spectral convention in
132	  Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} and the identity $\int p_\epsilon(y)e^{-i\xi\cdot
133	  y}\ud y = e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2/2}$ gives exactly the right side
134	  of~\eqref{E:variational-heat-envelope} as a distribution. The heat kernel is
135	  even, so either Fourier sign gives that same Gaussian multiplier. Its spectral
136	  integral is absolutely finite and continuous in $x$ by dominated convergence.
137	  Thus, equality of the two continuous distributions gives equality at every
138	  $x$, without an extra normalization factor. The physical convolution is
139	  nonnegative. Evenness of $\mu$ makes the spectral integral real, and its
140	  absolute value is bounded by its total Gaussian mass, the value at zero.
141	  Finally, $\Gamma \ne 0$ and $p_\epsilon > 0$ give strict positivity there.
142	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-heat-envelope}.
143	\end{proof}
144	
145	\begin{lemma}[Global regularity of the original mean]
146	  \label{L:variational-global-mean}
147	  Every mixed time and space derivative of $h_s$ is globally bounded in space,
148	  uniformly on compact time intervals. In particular, for $I = [0,1]$ there are
149	  finite constants $M,C_\Psi$ such that
150	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-global-mean}
151	    0\le h_s(x)\le M,\qquad
152	    \|h_s-h_t\|_\infty\le C_\Psi|s-t|,
153	    \qquad s,t\in I.
154	  \end{equation}
155	\end{lemma}
156	
157	\begin{proof}
158	  Extend $\Psi$ by zero in time; its compact support inside $(0,1)$ makes this a
159	  smooth extension. For any mixed derivative $D\Psi$, a fixed $\epsilon > 0$ and
160	  compactness of its common spatial support give $|D\Psi(t,x)| \le
161	  C_Dp_\epsilon(x)$ for all $t,x$. Here the heat kernel has a positive minimum
162	  on that support. Lemma~\ref{L:variational-heat-envelope} consequently bounds
163	  $\Gamma*|D\Psi(t,\cdot)|$ uniformly in $t,x$. Ordinary local differentiation
164	  against the Radon measure gives the corresponding derivatives of the
165	  convolution. After the change $r = s-t$,
166	  \[
167	    h_s(x)=\int_\R |r|^{-a}
168	    (\Gamma*\Psi(s-r,\cdot))(x)\ud r.
169	  \]
170	  For $s$ in a compact interval the relevant $r$ lie in a fixed bounded
171	  interval. The preceding global bound times $|r|^{-a}$ is integrable since $a <
172	  1$. Every derivative thus falls on the smooth test and passes through the
173	  integral by dominated convergence, with the claimed global spatial bounds.
174	  Nonnegativity follows from positive kernels. The bounded time derivative
175	  proves the Lipschitz estimate. No directional decay of the mean has been
176	  inferred. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-global-mean}.
177	\end{proof}

179	\begin{proposition}[The unmasked Rayleigh rate]
180	  \label{P:variational-unmasked-rate}
181	  On complex $L^2(\R^d)$, the operator $H_s = -\Delta-h_s$ is self-adjoint on
182	  $H^2$, with form domain $H^1$ and form $q_s(f) = \|\nabla f\|_2^2-\int
183	  h_s|f|^2$. Its spectral bottom $E_s$ is uniformly negative on $I$. The
184	  positive rate $\lambda_{\Psi,s} = \sqrt{-E_s}$ satisfies
185	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-real-rayleigh}
186	    \lambda_{\Psi,s}^2
187	    =\sup_{\substack{f\in H^1(\R^d;\R)\\\|f\|_2=1}}
188	    \left(\int h_sf^2-\|\nabla f\|_2^2\right).
189	  \end{equation}
190	  It is Lipschitz on $I$, and $I_\Psi: = \int_0^1\lambda_{\Psi,s}\ud s$ is
191	  positive and finite. No eigenstate at the unmasked bottom is asserted.
192	\end{proposition}
193	
194	\begin{proof}
195	  The Fourier Laplacian $A = -\Delta$ is self-adjoint on $H^2$, being
196	  multiplication by $|\xi|^2$ with its maximal domain. Multiplication $B_s =
197	  -h_s$ is bounded self-adjoint with norm at most $M$. Thus, $H_s = A+B_s$ is
198	  densely defined, symmetric and closed on $H^2$; the two graph norms are
199	  equivalent under a bounded perturbation. For real $b > M$,
200	  \[
201	    H_s-ib=(I+B_s(A-ib)^{-1})(A-ib).
202	  \]
203	  The first factor has a Neumann inverse because $\|B_s(A-ib)^{-1}\| \le M/b <
204	  1$, and the same holds with $+ib$. To check self-adjointness directly, for $u
205	  \in D(H_s^*)$ solve $(H_s-ib)v = (H_s^*-ib)u$ with $v \in D(H_s)$. Then $u-v
206	  \in \ker(H_s^*-ib) = \operatorname{Ran}(H_s+ib)^\perp = \{0\}$. Hence,
207	  $D(H_s^*) = D(H_s)$.
208	
209	  Set $c_{\mathrm{shift}} = 1+M$ and $J_s = H_s+c_{\mathrm{shift}} \ge 1$.
210	  Integration by parts on $H^2$ gives
211	  \[
212	    \|J_s^{1/2}f\|_2^2=q_s(f)+c_{\mathrm{shift}}\|f\|_2^2,\qquad
213	    \|f\|_{H^1}^2\le\|J_s^{1/2}f\|_2^2
214	    \le c_{\mathrm{shift}}\|f\|_{H^1}^2.
215	  \]
216	  Spectral cutoffs $1_{[1,n]}(J_s)$ show that $H^2 = D(J_s)$ is a core for the
217	  half-power norm; Fourier cutoffs give its density in $H^1$. Completion in the
218	  equivalent norms identifies $D(J_s^{1/2})$ and $H^1$ as $L^2$ subspaces, since
219	  both norms dominate $L^2$. This proves the stated form domain.
220	
221	  The spectral lower bound gives one direction of the Rayleigh identity. For the
222	  reverse, nonzero spectral projections in $[E_s,E_s+\epsilon]$ give unit $H^2$
223	  vectors with Rayleigh values at most $E_s+\epsilon$. The bottom is finite
224	  because the operator is bounded below and has finite Rayleigh tests. Let
225	  $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Real tests give the same infimum: $q_s(u+iv) =
226	  q_s(u)+q_s(v)$, so the quotient is the norm-weighted average of the nonzero
227	  real quotients. This proves the Rayleigh identity with $-E_s$ on the left. The
228	  following negative upper bound justifies writing that value as
229	  $\lambda_{\Psi,s}^2$ in~\eqref{E:variational-real-rayleigh}.
230	
231	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-original-common-trial} supplies, for this original
232	  $\Psi$, one unit compactly supported $w$ and a finite plateau mask with a
233	  common strictly negative upper bound $\epsilon_0 > 0$. Its trial has support
234	  in $B_{2L}$; choose its plateau radius $R_0 \ge 2L$. The unmasked form on this
235	  same $w$ is no larger. Consequently, $-M \le E_s \le -\epsilon_0 < 0$, and
236	  $\sqrt{\epsilon_0} \le \lambda_{\Psi,s} \le \sqrt M$. Comparing identical unit
237	  form tests gives $|E_s-E_t| \le \|h_s-h_t\|_\infty$ and therefore
238	  \[
239	    |\lambda_{\Psi,s}-\lambda_{\Psi,t}|
240	    \le \frac{C_\Psi}{2\sqrt{\epsilon_0}}|s-t|.
241	  \]
242	  This also proves positivity and finiteness of $I_\Psi$. No compact-potential
243	  spectral theorem was applied to $H_s$. This proves
244	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-unmasked-rate}.
245	\end{proof}

247	\subsection{Removing masks from the numerical lower rate}
248	
249	\begin{proposition}[Monotone rates and the original point moment]
250	  \label{P:variational-remove-mask}
251	  There is an increasing family of admissible radial masks $m_R$ tending to one,
252	  for which the compact ground rates satisfy
253	  $\lambda_{R,s}\uparrow\lambda_{\Psi,s}$ uniformly on $I$ as $R \to \infty$,
254	  with the compact ground statements used for $R \ge R_0(\Psi)$. For the
255	  original canonical solution and any fixed $x$,
256	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}
257	    \liminf_{T\to\infty}T^{-\kappa}\log\E|u(T,x)|^2
258	    \ge2I_\Psi-\frac{v_\Psi}{2}.
259	  \end{equation}
260	\end{proposition}
261	
262	\begin{proof}
263	  Put $F(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$ and zero otherwise, and define
264	  \[
265	    \chi(r)=\frac{F(2-r)}{F(2-r)+F(r-1)},\qquad
266	    m_R(x)=\chi(|x|/R).
267	  \]
268	  The denominator is positive. The numerator decreases and the second
269	  denominator term increases; thus $\chi$ is nonincreasing, equals one on $r \le
270	  1$, and zero on $r \ge 2$. Flatness of $F$ at zero gives smoothness. Since
271	  $\chi$ is constant near zero, $m_R$ is smooth also at the spatial origin.
272	  These even $[0,1]$ masks increase pointwise to one.
273	
274	  Choose $R_0$ so the preceding common trial lies in the plateau. Every $R \ge
275	  R_0$ has the same negative margin. For each fixed $R$, the compact-family
276	  theorem applies to $m_Rh_s$. Its real Rayleigh formula follows from the same
277	  real/complex quotient argument as~\eqref{E:variational-real-rayleigh}. The
278	  rates are continuous, positive, at most $\sqrt M$ and monotone in $R$. For
279	  every fixed real unit $f \in H^1$, dominated convergence gives $\int m_Rh_sf^2
280	  \to \int h_sf^2$. Hence,
281	  \[
282	    \sup_{R\ge R_0}\lambda_{R,s}^2
283	    =\sup_{\|f\|_2=1,\ f\in H^1(\R^d;\R)}
284	    \sup_{R\ge R_0}
285	    \left(\int m_Rh_sf^2-\|\nabla f\|_2^2\right)
286	    =\lambda_{\Psi,s}^2.
287	  \]
288	  Only two numerical suprema were interchanged. Positive square roots give the
289	  pointwise rate convergence. For $R_n = R_0+n$ and $\epsilon > 0$, the
290	  increasing open sets $\{s:\lambda_{\Psi,s}-\lambda_{R_n,s}<\epsilon\}$ cover
291	  compact $I$. A finite subcover lies in the largest one, proving uniform
292	  convergence. Monotonicity extends it to all real $R \to \infty$. Therefore,
293	  $\int_I\lambda_{R,s}\ud s\uparrow I_\Psi$.
294	
295	  At each fixed $R$ use this very same mask in the operator path and mean when
296	  applying Proposition~\ref{P:raw-block-original-lower}. It gives the lower
297	  bound with $2\int_I\lambda_{R,s}\ud s-v_\Psi/2$ for the same original point
298	  liminf. Taking the numerical supremum over these individual bounds proves
299	  \eqref{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}. There is no $R(T)$, unmasked noisy
300	  wave, uniform-in-mask Gaussian estimate or exchange of source and time limits.
301	  This proves Proposition~\ref{P:variational-remove-mask}.
302	\end{proof}

304	\subsection{Full-class dilation and finite variational values for nonnegative controls}
305	
306	\begin{lemma}[Radon and Rayleigh dilation]\label{L:variational-control-dilation}
307	  For $r > 0$ the map
308	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-control-dilation}
309	    (D_r\Psi)(s,x)=r^{d+2-\alpha}\Psi(s,rx)
310	  \end{equation}
311	  is a bijection of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}$, with inverse $D_{1/r}$. With
312	  the same original covariance,
313	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-dilation-values}
314	    h_{D_r\Psi,s}(x)=r^2h_{\Psi,s}(rx),\qquad
315	    v_{D_r\Psi}=r^{4-\alpha}v_\Psi,\qquad
316	    \lambda_{D_r\Psi,s}=r\lambda_{\Psi,s},\quad
317	    I_{D_r\Psi}=rI_\Psi.
318	  \end{equation}
319	\end{lemma}
320	
321	\begin{proof}
322	  Positive dilation preserves the full smooth positive nonzero class;
323	  multiplication of its amplitude powers gives the stated inverse. Homogeneity
324	  of the physical Radon measure gives, for every nonnegative measurable $G$,
325	  \[
326	    \int G(ry)\Gamma(\ud y)
327	    =r^{\alpha-d}\int G(z)\Gamma(\ud z).
328	  \]
329	  Indeed, its left pushforward measure on a Borel set $A$ is $\Gamma(A/r) =
330	  r^{\alpha-d}\Gamma(A)$. Positive Tonelli applies this identity inside the
331	  temporal convolution, giving $h_{D_r\Psi,s}(x) = r^2h_{\Psi,s}(rx)$. Now use
332	  the \emph{Lebesgue} substitution $z = rx$ in the original pairing:
333	  \[
334	    v_{D_r\Psi}=r^{d+2-\alpha}r^2r^{-d}v_\Psi
335	    =r^{4-\alpha}v_\Psi.
336	  \]
337	  This distinguishes the Radon pushforward from the spatial volume factor; it
338	  includes singular covariances and white noise.
339	
340	  The map $U_rf(x) = r^{d/2}f(rx)$ is a unitary bijection on real $L^2$,
341	  preserving $H^1,H^2$ as sets under its inverse. Weak derivatives give
342	  $\|\nabla U_rf\|_2^2 = r^2\|\nabla f\|_2^2$ and $\int h_{D_r\Psi,s}(U_rf)^2 =
343	  r^2\int h_{\Psi,s}f^2$. The real Rayleigh bijection proves the squared rate
344	  identity; the rates are positive, so their square roots and integrals give
345	  \eqref{E:variational-dilation-values}. On $H^2$ this is also $H_{D_r\Psi,s}U_r
346	  = r^2U_rH_{\Psi,s}$. Time has not been rescaled. For compact masks the
347	  corresponding identity uses $m_R(rx) = m_{R/r}(x)$; a fixed mask radius is not
348	  invariant. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-control-dilation}.
349	\end{proof}
350	
351	\begin{proposition}[Intrinsic variational lower bounds]
352	  \label{P:variational-positive-scores}
353	  For $c > 0$, the set of variational values
354	  $\{cI_\Psi-v_\Psi/2:\Psi\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}\}$ is nonempty and
355	  bounded above. Its finite real supremum $S_c^{\mathrm{pos}}$ is positive and
356	  satisfies
357	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-score-homogeneity}
358	    S_c^{\mathrm{pos}}=c^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}S_1^{\mathrm{pos}},
359	    \qquad
360	    Q_2\ge S_2^{\mathrm{pos}},
361	  \end{equation}
362	  where $Q_2$ is the original point liminf. The coefficient-one value is an
363	  auxiliary variational value; no first-moment or source-constant identification
364	  is asserted.
365	\end{proposition}
366	
367	\begin{proof}
368	  Write $k = 3-\alpha > 0$, $q = 4-\alpha = k+1$ and $m = q/k > 1$. Fix one
369	  $\Psi_0$ from the nonempty class and put $I_0 = I_{\Psi_0} > 0$, $v_0 =
370	  v_{\Psi_0} > 0$. Positivity of the latter is
371	  Lemma~\ref{L:compact-raw-profile}. For $r_0 = (I_0/v_0)^{1/k} > 0$, which need
372	  not be less than one, the exact real-power identity gives
373	  \[
374	    I_{D_{r_0}\Psi_0}-v_{D_{r_0}\Psi_0}/2
375	    =r_0I_0-r_0^qv_0/2=r_0I_0/2>0.
376	  \]
377	  This positive value is obtained from a smooth nonnegative control.
378	
379	  For $c > 0$ put $r_c = c^{1/k}$ and $K_c = c^m > 0$.
380	  Lemma~\ref{L:variational-control-dilation} and the exact scalar powers give,
381	  for every $\Psi$,
382	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-score-set-scaling}
383	    cI_{D_{r_c}\Psi}-v_{D_{r_c}\Psi}/2
384	    =K_c(I_\Psi-v_\Psi/2).
385	  \end{equation}
386	  Since $D_{r_c}$ is a bijection of the entire class, the whole set of
387	  variational values with coefficient $c$ is $K_c$ times the whole
388	  coefficient-one set of variational values.
389	
390	  We prove boundedness before taking finite-real suprema. The independent
391	  Theorem~\ref{T:full-upper}, for the \emph{same canonical solution}, gives
392	  \[
393	    \E|u(T,0)|^2\le e(T+2)^d e^{C_{\mathrm{up}}T^\kappa},
394	    \qquad T\ge1,\quad C_{\mathrm{up}}<\infty.
395	  \]
396	  Its prefactor is negligible: choose $\epsilon = \kappa/2 > 0$, use $\log T \le
397	  (T^\epsilon-1)/\epsilon$ and $\log(T+2) \le \log T+\log3$ for $T \ge 1$, and
398	  divide by $T^\kappa$. Thus, the original point limsup is at most
399	  $C_{\mathrm{up}}$. One fixed test/mask lower bound gives a finite lower bound
400	  for $Q_2$, so $Q_2$ is finite. By~\eqref{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}
401	  every coefficient-two variational expression is at most this same $Q_2 \le
402	  C_{\mathrm{up}}$, uniformly in $\Psi$.
403	  Equation~\eqref{E:variational-score-set-scaling} at $c = 2$ consequently
404	  bounds all coefficient-one variational values by $C_{\mathrm{up}}/K_2$. The
405	  nonempty set has a finite real supremum $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}} > 0$ by the
406	  positive test above.
407	
408	  For general $c$, set equality and $K_c > 0$ show that $K_cS_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$
409	  is the supremum: it is an upper bound, and every smaller number is exceeded by
410	  $K_c$ times a coefficient-one variational expression within the corresponding
411	  positive distance of its supremum. This proves finiteness, positivity and the
412	  first identity in~\eqref{E:variational-score-homogeneity}. Taking the
413	  numerical supremum of the coefficient-two lower bounds proves the second.
414	  Although $2^m > 2$, the resulting $S_2^{\mathrm{pos}} > 2S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$
415	  is only a comparison of auxiliary variational values. It is not a Jensen
416	  improvement without a first-moment identification. This proves
417	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-positive-scores}.
418	\end{proof}
419	
420	For $\Gamma = 0$, the mean, original variance and Rayleigh rate are zero. Set
421	all these variational values to zero; the free canonical solution $u = 1$ has
422	the corresponding zero moment rate. Strict positivity above is restricted to
423	nonzero covariance. Matching an upper variational rate and identifying an exact
424	pointwise limit remain later steps.

431	\begin{equation}\label{E:theta-envelope}
432	    \E X_n(t,x)^2\le P_n e^{2\theta t}C^n\theta^{-2n},
433	    \qquad\theta\ge\theta_0.
434	  \end{equation}
435	  For the finite-spectral-measure hypothesis in
